questions.title: A coherent view of Adam and the Serpent
questions.content:
# A coherent view of Adam and the Serpent ## Frage

I was debating with Biblical literalists, and I struggled to present a coherent view of Genesis 3.

  1. It starts with "וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם מִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה" ("And the serpent was the shrewdest of all the wild beasts), meaning that it was one of its species.
  2. Adam named all the field animals, knowing their nature.
  3. According to Yevamos 63a, Adam knew all [kinds of] animals intimately.
  4. Ergo, Adam met the Serpent and knew its nature.

I was confused here — if Adam had known the Serpent's evil intentions, I suppose he would have acted accordingly. Since he didn't, and given the sages' respect for his wisdom, I can only think that, in fact, the Serpent's nature was to tell the truth:

"And the serpent said to the woman, 'You are not going to die, but God knows that as soon as you eat of it your eyes will be opened and you will be like divine beings who know good and bad.'”

Is there a source that reconciles the Biblical verses with rabbinic Midrashim in a non-contradicting way?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 2)

At face value, Adam may have known all the animals and their nature, but we have no evidence that Chava had any of this knowledge. The Serpent convinced/tricked Chava who in turn caused Adam to sin. There is no indication that Adam had any interaction with the Serpent during this episode.

Bereishis Rabbah 19:3 discusses Adam's whereabouts during this episode

וַתֹּאמֶר הָאִשָּׁה אֶל הַנָּחָשׁ (בראשית ג, ב), וְהֵיכָן הָיָה אָדָם בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה, אַבָּא בַּר קוֹרְיָיה אָמַר נִתְעַסֵּק בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיָשַׁן לוֹ. רַבָּנָן אַמְרֵי נְטָלוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְהֶחֱזִירוֹ בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, אָמַר לוֹ כָּאן בֵּית נֶטַע, כָּאן בֵּית זֶרַע, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (ירמיה ב, ו): בְּאֶרֶץ לֹא עָבַר בָּהּ אִישׁ וְלֹא יָשַׁב אָדָם שָׁם, לֹא יָשַׁב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שָׁם.

“The woman said to the serpent: From the fruit of the trees of the garden we may eat” (Genesis 3:2). “The woman said to the serpent” – where was Adam at that time? Abba bar Korya said: He had engaged in the way of nature and he was sleeping. The Rabbis say: The Holy One blessed be He was taking him and circulating throughout the entire world [telling him]: ‘This is a good place to plant, this is a good place to sow.’ That is what is written: “In a land that no man has ever crossed, and where no person [adam] has ever dwelled” (Jeremiah 2:6) – Adam the first man did not dwell there.

Pirkei DeRebbi Eliezer 13:5 dicusses the Serpents plan

דָּן דִּין נָחָשׁ בֵּינוֹ לְבֵין עַצְמוֹ וְאָמַר: אִם הוֹלֵךְ אֲנִי וְאוֹמֵר לְאָדָם, יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵעַ לִי, שֶׁהָאִישׁ לְעוֹלָם קָשֶׁה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְהָאִישׁ רַע מַעֲלָלִים״. אֶלָּא הוֹלֵךְ אֲנִי וְאוֹמֵר לְחַוָּה, שֶׁהָאִשָּׁה שֶׁאֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהִיא שׁוֹמַעַת לִי, שֶׁהַנָּשִׁים נִשְׁמָעוֹת לְכָל הַבְּרִיּוֹת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״פְּתַיּוּת וּבַל יָדְעָה מָּה״.

The serpent argued with itself, saying: If I go and speak to Adam, I know that he will not listen to me, for a man is always hard (to be persuaded), as it is said, "For a man is churlish and evil in his doings" (1 Sam. 25:3); but behold I will speak to Eve, for I know that she will listen to me; for women listen to all creatures, as it is said, "She is simple and knoweth nothing" (Prov. 9:18).

### Antwort 2 (Score: 1)

The problem with most interpretations is that they don't ask the questions the text asks. Such as: How does the snake know what the tree of knowledge will do to Eve?

I think most people accept the idea of the snake being Satan because it kind of answers that question by writing it off as secret knowledge by the adversary. This answer is not very satisfying.

I believe the only way to understand this story is to read it literally and without putting any religious notions on it whether you are Jewish, Christian, or Muslim. I think we often make the mistake of not letting the Torah worldbuild because we're too preoccupied looking for lofty spiritual answers. I think if you let the logic of the text flow then the story is quite understandable but possibly not religiously satisfying to anyone.

Josephus and Jubilees both state that all animals spoke one language with humans in the beginning. Jubilees makes the claim this ability was lost after Adam ate from the Tree. Abarbanel in his commentary to Genesis 3:1 says that the snake never spoke. Because the Torah lists punishments and taking away speech was not listed and it's the only one really worth mentioning. His answer seems to be addressing and defeating Jubilees and Josephus. But a rare book of tosafot collections called Moshav Zekenim says that the universal language that all life spoke was lost when all languages were confused in the Tower of Babel story. Which means that all animals spoke in the garden of eden story, the noahs ark story (I mean just logistically doesn't that story make so much more sense if all the animals and humans could talk to each other?), all the way up til the tower of Babel. This also explains why the Bible doesn't say God had to open the mouth of the snake to talk, but had to open the mouth of the donkey because it happens after the tower of Babel.

We don't know if Abarbanel knew of this opinion from Moshav Zekeinim but he offers a fascinating alternative to talking animals that I argue answers the question of how the snake knows what the fruit does.

According to Abarbanel Eve saw the serpent eat from the tree of knowledge day after day and it wasn't dying, which is what God told Adam would happen. From there the Torah is basically reflecting her inner monologue and she convinces herself the fruit looks good to eat. But Abarbanel still doesn't answer how the Serpent or Eve know what the tree does because God never says what it does, only that on the day the human eats of it he will surely die.

I think Abarbanel is correct, the snake does eat the fruit day after day, and that's why the snake knows what the fruit does: because it did it to him. This also explains why there's wordplay with Arum/Nakedness happening.

Genesis 2:25-3:8 (Abridged)

וַיִּֽהְי֤וּ שְׁנֵיהֶם֙ עֲרוּמִּ֔ים הָֽאָדָ֖ם וְאִשְׁתּ֑וֹ וְלֹ֖א יִתְבֹּשָֽׁשׁוּ׃

The two of them were naked/arumim, the Human and his wife,

yet they felt no shame.

וְהַנָּחָשׁ֙ הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם מִכֹּל֙ חַיַּ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה יְהֹוָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אֶל־הָ֣אִשָּׁ֔ה אַ֚ף כִּֽי־אָמַ֣ר אֱלֹהִ֔ים לֹ֣א תֹֽאכְל֔וּ מִכֹּ֖ל עֵ֥ץ הַגָּֽן׃

Now the serpent was the shrewdest/arum of all the wild beasts that God יהוה had made. It said to the woman, “Did God really say: You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?”

.... וַתִּפָּקַ֙חְנָה֙ עֵינֵ֣י שְׁנֵיהֶ֔ם וַיֵּ֣דְע֔וּ כִּ֥י עֵֽירֻמִּ֖ם הֵ֑ם וַֽיִּתְפְּרוּ֙ עֲלֵ֣ה תְאֵנָ֔ה וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ

לָהֶ֖ם חֲגֹרֹֽת׃

Then the eyes of both of them were opened and they perceived that they were naked/arum; and they sewed together fig leaves and made themselves loincloths.

The serpent knowing good from evil helps explain why he's Arum/Naked just like Adam and Eve become at the end of the story. It also explains how it was able to have the moral nuance to sway Eve with a single question and be punished by God as if an animal can be held morally responsible. It also explains how the donkey was able to plead a moral case against Balaam for striking her instead of knowing her better from a shared history together.

I think the deeper message of the story is that the tree of knowledge makes you believe you know right from wrong. This knowledge is apparently allowed to God and animals, but not to humans. Something apparently really bad will happen if we believe we know right from wrong. Narratively it's not a shock when the next story is brothers killing each other and God has to wipe out humanity less than 10 chapters later. It seems the Torah was spot on: us believing we know right from wrong made really bad things happen.

All this to say, the story is really about a snake who wanted to lead Eve astray. And it really just talked to her. And the story is more about how unified all life was, how the tree of life was offered to everyone unless humans ate from the tree of knowledge. Because can you imagine if the generation of Noah, the generation God had to wipe out, could live forever?

questions.title: What happened to Jephthah's daughter?
questions.content:
# What happened to Jephthah's daughter? ## Frage

You know the story. Jephthah, before going into battle, promises to God as a burnt offering the first thing that comes out of his house to meet him. God gives him victory, he comes home, his only daughter runs out to meet him, and... what?

I'm aware of two interpretations (in Christian circles):

  • "burnt offering" means that something is dedicated in entirety to God. Jephthah's daughter was dedicated to serving God and remained a virgin.
  • Jephthah made a foolish vow and foolishly carried it out. He should have gone to a priest to be released from his vow. Instead, he committed the crime of human sacrifice.

The question: what do Jewish sources say on the topic? Is there a debate between the two versions above (or a third option?) among Jewish commentators, and which (if either) is generally accepted?

## Antworten ### ✅ Antwort 1 (Score: 2)

Ibn Ezra and the Radak suggest that Jephthah meant that the first thing to come out the door would be sacrificed only if it was an “appropriate” creature. But if so, why were Jephthah and his daughter so worked up about the vow? Because, if a sacrifice wasn’t “appropriate”, the creature would still have to be consecrated to God. So the daughter had to seclude herself in a house outside the city, in nun-like fashion.

Later medieval commentators (such as Abravanel, Gersonides, or Malbim) agreed that Jephthah only consecrated his daughter to God as a virgin. Indeed, the Bible says: “And he did to her as he had vowed. She had never known a man.” Why add that last comment? It must be because it is relevant. However, asceticism and lifelong virginity are not encouraged in Judaism.

### Antwort 2 (Score: 1)

Ramban says that he made a mistake and sacrificed her. He also quotes ibn Ezra that he dedicated her to God and never allowed her to marry or mingle with people, censuring it.

And this was the mistake that Jephthah made with his daughter. For he thought that just as a cheirem ["doomed" object] of the chief of Israel is valid and takes effect to put [certain] people to death, and [also] anyone who transgresses it is liable to the death-penalty, so [Jephthah thought] that if he uttered a vow at a time of war, to make an offering of a certain person or persons, the vow is valid; but he did not know that a cheirem declared by the king and Sanhedrin is valid [only] regarding the destruction of rebels, or against one who transgresses their decrees and ordinances. But that a vow should take effect to make a burnt-offering of something not appropriate for G-d, [as Jephthah thought] — Heaven forbid! Therefore the Rabbis have said in Bereshith Rabbah that [Jephthah] was not even obliged to pay the price of her market-value to the Temple treasury [as his vow was totally invalid], and he was punished for her [innocent] blood!

Now do not let yourself be misled by Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra's empty words, when he says that the meaning of the expression and I will offer it up for a burnt-offering is "or I will offer it up," as if to say: "if that which comes forth of the doors of my house be a man or woman, that person shall be holy to G-d, inasmuch as he will abstain from the ways of the world, to stand to minister in the Name of the Eternal in prayer and thanksgiving to G-d; but if it be something fit for an offering, I will make it a burnt-offering." Accordingly [Ibn Ezra's interpretation continues, since Jephthah's daughter was the first to come out to meet her father], he built her a house outside the city where she resided in seclusion, and he provided her with sustenance all her days, and no man knew her, so that his daughter remained shut away [from the world all her life].

All this are words of emptiness. For if he vowed that [whatsoever comes forth of the door of his house] shall be the Eternal's, this does not mean that he should be a recluse [from the world], but instead he is to be like Samuel, of whom his mother said, and I shall give him unto the Eternal, and he was a servant in the House of G-d, not a recluse. And according to the ordinances of the Torah, no man can utter a vow which will bind the persons who come out of the door of his house to live thereafter in seclusion, just as he cannot bring them as an offering. And if the matter be so [as Ibn Ezra put it] then Jephthah's daughter would be bewailing her virginity with her companions with her, like harlots enhancing their hire! Heaven forbid that this be a custom in Israel, to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year because she did not marry and she worshipped G-d in purity! Rather, this whole subject is to be understood in its plain meaning [that Jephthah actually brought her as an offering], and his mistake was as I have explained.

questions.title: The practice of Jews keeping dogs
questions.content:
# The practice of Jews keeping dogs ## Frage

Do the verses (Ex 11.7) "But not a dog shall snarl at any of the Israelites, at human or beast..." and (Ex 22.30) "you must not eat flesh torn by beasts in the field; you shall cast it to the dogs..." imply that the Jews in Egypt owned/kept dogs?

What do Jewish sources tell us about the use or domestication of dogs in Biblical or rabbinic times? How common was the practice?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 1)

There are many laws about dogs, such as feeding them the meat of dead animals. Dogs eating human fecal matter on the Sabbath. How and when dangerous dogs must be chained, how to deal with guard dogs and much more. So it seems fairly common as an almost work animal, but as a pet, they seem to dissuade raising non Kosher animals. There is also talk of a dogs dedication to man and Ben Yehoyada notes in the name of the sages that Kelev is a contraction of Kuloi Lev = All heart.(Horayot 13a)

An interesting tidbit is in Talmud Eruvin 81a where it mentions the Amorah Shmuel feeding Ezekiel bread to HIS dog, not A dog.

אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב: מְעָרְבִין בְּפַת עֲדָשִׁים. אִינִי?! וְהָא הָהִיא דַּהֲוַאי בִּשְׁנֵי דְּמָר שְׁמוּאֵל, וְשַׁדְיַיהּ לְכַלְבֵּיהּ וְלָא אַכְלַהּ!
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin said that Rav said: One may establish an eiruv with lentil bread. The Gemara raises a difficulty: Is that so? Is such bread edible? But there was that lentil bread in the days of Mar Shmuel, which he threw to his dog, and even it would not eat it. Clearly, lentil bread is not fit for human consumption.

### Antwort 2 (Score: 1)

It is related that when Dovid HaMelech was niftar on a hot Shabbos day that dogs which he owned were locked up to protect him from them. I know that I read this- but perhaps someone can bring the source as I don't remember it.

questions.title: Are soulmates in a relationship that lasts forever
questions.content:
# Are soulmates in a relationship that lasts forever ## Frage

Is a soulmate just a helper for this life, or does the Kabbalah or the Zohar etc. say the union is bound together even in heaven, meaning a relationship that lasts forever?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 4)

Soulmates are two halves (or parts) of the same soul, and are absolutely formed in heaven, and indeed, remain together post-resurrection in Olam Haba (unless they divorce of course). This fact is recognised in Kabbalah and even some areas of Halacha:

Kabbalah sources:

Quotes from Zohar chapters 30 & 32, I 91a onwards:

All the figures of souls that are to be born stand before God in pairs.

When their time of marriage arrives... God... joins them as at first, and proclaims their union. Thus when they are joined they become one body and one soul, right and left in unison, and in this way 'there is nothing new under the sun'.

Happy are the righteous whose souls are beatified before the Holy King before they come into this world... all souls are formed into pairs of male and female, and thus united.

When God sends souls into the world they are formed into pairs of male and female, and thus united... After that they are separated, and subsequently taken down among mankind … When their time of marriage arrives... He joins them as at first.

See this answer: https://judaism.stackexchange.com/a/149861/31534

Chesed LeAvraham 2:65 discusses the ins and outs of destined matches and how they can be "lost forever" and what to do to avoid that, so they can indeed be forever.

See this Torah.org page which brings practically the entire teachings of the Arizal on soul mates: https://torah.org/torah-portion/perceptions-5765-chayeisarah/

Halacha sources:

Moed Katan 18b discusses halachot related to zivugim, although it doesn't explicitly discuss them being eternal. It does frame them as set in heaven before birth, which as we know from above is because they are two halves of the same soul.

The following halachot discuss who a wife will reunite with if her first husband dies and she remarries, after resurrection:

Hagahot Yad Sha’ul (YD 366:3) – “a woman will reunite with her second husband after the resurrection.”

Zera Emet, YD 146, etc. – if she had children with both, she reunites with her first husband in Heaven.

Piskei Teshuva 124 (per Rav Aviner’s reading) – a wife is reunited with the first husband, unless the second marriage was more distinctly successful.

Chatam Sofer – second marriage can nullify the prior bond (post-resurrection).

See this question and its sources: Soul mates, death and remarriage - who will we spend eternity with?

(I partially utilised ChatGPT to check the answers that I quoted to distil the information from them, and then proofed it before posting this answer)

### ✅ Antwort 2 (Score: 2)

There are sources that would point to the union being "bound together even in heaven".

Refer to the Gemara in several places e.g. Sanhedrin 22a:

וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם קוֹדֶם יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד, בַּת קוֹל יוֹצֵאת וְאוֹמֶרֶת ״בַּת פְּלוֹנִי לִפְלוֹנִי״

But doesn’t Rav Yehuda say that Rav says: Forty days before the formation of the fetus a Divine Voice emerges and states: The daughter of so-and-so shall be the wife of so-and-so?

questions.title: Medieval criticism of Rambam's program of providing reasons for the commandments
questions.content:
# Medieval criticism of Rambam's program of providing reasons for the commandments ## Frage

Rambam spends a large part of the third section of the guide giving reasons for the commandments in line with his rationalist outlook.

There are Rishonim that weren't pleased with some of the reasons given (e.g., for korbanos).

I'm not looking for that.

Should it exist, as I seem to recall it does, I'm looking for explicit criticism by rishonim of his entire project of rationalizing the mitzvos.

Specifically, that anchoring them in human reason may lead to their neglect should people decide that a given mitzvah's reason isn't applicable to them or should societal norms change rendering a given mitzvah irrelevant based on Maimonides' rationale.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 2)

As far as I know, there is no criticism of the concept of giving reasons for the commandments as such, but there are views that are arguably opposed to details of the Rambam's program. As in the view that it's better to accept the mitzvot without investigating the reasons, and discovering the reasons is only the second best option (Kuzari 2:26). Or the view that the mitzvot are intended to bring about a spiritual benefit (הענין האלהי) rather than a worldly benefit (Ran, Derashot 11). Or the tendency to offer symbolic reasons instead of practical ones (as far as I can tell this is a tendency, not that anyone has actually claimed all the mitzvot are explicable only by mystical reasons and none by rational reasons; the Rambam also sometimes gives symbolic reasons, e.g. More Nevuchim 3:46).

As far as I know, the view that there are no reasons for the commandments doesn't exist among the Rishonim. This has been claimed, so it might be worth explaining the reason why I don't think it's correct. Lorberbaum believes that there was opposition to giving reasons for the commandments in the Rambam's time, based on his description in More Nevuchim 3:31 of people who would prefer that there would be no reason at all for the mitzvot (והטוב אצלם שלא יושכל למצוה ולאזהרה ענין כלל). This seems to me to be a misreading, because firstly, the Rambam is describing a feeling or tendency, but not an articulated theory (חלי שימצאוהו בנפשם ולא יוכלו להגות בו ולא ידעו לומר אותו). Secondly, the Rambam says that the view that the mitzvot have a reason is the opinion of all Jews (More Nevuchim 3:31). Apparently then this view is insignificant enough to be excluded from "all Jews," if he meant it was a Jewish view at all. However, he also quotes the Rambam's commentators, such as Narboni, who identify this view with that of "religious people" (תוריים), which is more likely to be an actual Jewish view, but apparently not a view that has come down to us from a proponent.

Lorberbaum also wants to identify this view that the mitzvot are unknowable with that of the Tur, and suggests that the Tur is possibly concerned that offering reasons for the commandments based on historical context (as the Rambam does in this case) would lead to disrespect towards the prohibitions (p. 40). Again both claims seem to me to be a misreading, since (1) the Tur, in one particular context, razing the beard, doesn't accept the Rambam's speculative reason that this was an idolatrous practice, and falls back to saying we don't need to know the reason, and no epistemological or pragmatic claim is being made at all. (2) If any general criticism is intended, then rather than speculatively positing a hitherto-unknown anti-reason community, it would be much more straightforward to identify the Tur's brief rejection with some known criticism of historical reasons, as that of the Ramban (a big influence on the Tur) in his commentary. (3) The Tur himself, in his (long) Torah commentary, does offer a practical reason. (4) This is also, as Fred notes in the comments to the question, the kind of thing that the Rambam himself says (Hilchot Meila 8:8, Hilchot Temura 4:13), and isn't expressing general opposition to finding reasons for commandments. If anything it should be read as an affirmation of the Rambam's approach, which he's only repeating as a commonplace.

There was very fierce controversy surrounding the Rambam in the generation after his death (even leading up to some of his books being burned). Some of the controversy involved the character of the mitzvot (it's not clear to me whether this was an issue of obligatoriness or merely of classification, i.e. that the mitzvot are in the same category of things as secular laws). However, as far as I know, none of those involved in the controversy took issue with the Rambam's views on the matter (or if they did they didn't leave behind writings). Typically they took the Rambam as being on their own side and took issue with his interpreters (see for instance קבוצת מכתבים בעניני המחלוקת... letter 7).

questions.title: How come Adam didn't know he's a different species?
questions.content:
# How come Adam didn't know he's a different species? ## Frage

In Bereishit 2:19–20, Adam names all the animals, and Chazal describe this as a display of his wisdom and insight.

At the same time, Sanhedrin 38b and Bereishit Rabbah 18:4 says that Adam even sought a mate among the animals and even attempted relations with them (Yevamot 63a) — until Hashem created Chavah.

If Adam was wise enough to perceive the essence of each creature to name them, why did he not recognize from the beginning that he was fundamentally a different species, requiring a partner of his own kind?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 8)

Like many questions on this site, this is predicated on a misunderstanding of sources, and then asking a question about it. Perhaps part of this is hastiness in not looking at sources, and blindly trusting ChatGPT output.

As far as I can tell:

  • Sanhedrin 38b merely says Adam named the animals
  • Bereishit Rabbah 18:4 (actually, an error for Bereishit Rabba 17:4) merely says that, aside from naming the animals, he saw that the animals were brought in pairs, and then wondered where his pair was.

Neither says that he sought a mate among the animals. (Did ChatGPT 5 hallucinate that these sources said this?)

Yes, one Tanna or Amora in Yevamot 63a, Rabbi Eleazar, interprets a verse that in his (perhaps subsequent) search for a mate, he had intercourse with every animal. The question then becomes -- "I have this specific view of how the world should work, and how an interpretation should be, but -- gasp! -- this Tanna or Amora has a different way of thinking about it. Isn't that strange? Now please account for it, either by acknowledging how wrong he was, or by reinterpreting it to conform with my framework". Sometimes this approach is legitimate, when the premise is readily acceptable. And sometimes is it not so legitimate. Regardless, it leads to dozens of questions being placed in short order, because they are so easy to devise.

Possible answers:

  1. Indeed, Rabbi Eleazar (ben Pedat) or Rabbi Eleazar (ben Shamua) was being silly. What nonsense!
  2. Rabbi Eleazar did not agree with the premise being read into the text that the naming reflected a deep understanding of the essence of each creature. Where do Chazal say this, and is Rabbi Eleazar among those who say it? Not all of Chazal need to agree.
  3. Grouped as it is in Yevamot among a corpus of Rabbi Eleazar statements, and other statements by others, where the theme is the relationship between a husband and wife, that was the import of Rabbi Eleazar's statement. He intended it as a derasha, homiletically, rather than a historical reading of the text.

questions.title: Importance of Adam naming animals
questions.content:
# Importance of Adam naming animals ## Frage

In Bereishit 2:19–20, Adam names the animals. Rashi (to v. 20) notes that he recognized their essence and named them accordingly.

As a simple answer to a child’s “Why is a cow called a cow?”, one might say: “Because Adam named it.” But from a more serious perspective:

  1. What would be the long-standing significance if Adam had chosen different names (e.g., calling a dog מַלְב instead of כֶּלֶב)?
  2. Could Adam have used names already found elsewhere in the Torah (assuming, per midrash, that the Torah pre-existed Creation)?

How would such scenarios affect our understanding of language, Torah, and creation?

questions.title: Suicide or abortion
questions.content:
# Suicide or abortion ## Frage

What is the halacha if (chalilah) a woman who is pregnant threatens suicide if she is not able to have an abortion? Do we allow (or mandate) an abortion? Do we ignore her statement? Another course of action? If the stage of development is a factor in the answer please indicate the differences.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 7)

From Aish:

Judaism recognizes psychiatric as well as physical factors in evaluating the potential threat that the fetus poses to the mother. The degree of mental illness that must be present to justify termination of a pregnancy has been widely debated by rabbinic scholars, without a clear consensus of opinion regarding the exact criteria for permitting abortion in such instances. Nevertheless, all agree that were a pregnancy to cause a woman to become suicidal, there would be grounds for abortion.

questions.title: Knowledge of God in Olam Haba/Olam HaNeshamot
questions.content:
# Knowledge of God in Olam Haba/Olam HaNeshamot ## Frage

In this world, there is room for doubt about the existence of God; it is at least conceivable (chas v’shalom) that there might not be a God. Many classical “proofs” for God — such as Rambam’s mechuyav ha-metziut (Necessary Being), or similar arguments in the Sefer HaIkkarim and in Chassidut — insist that the very concept of God is a logical imperative (notwithstanding the loose use of the word "logical" here, given that Hashem is beyond logic etc.).

My question is: In the future, when the veils of doubt are lifted and God is revealed without question, will that certainty come only from direct experience of His presence, or will it also include the intellectual clarity that His existence is logically necessary?

I think the latter is clearly the case, but I would be glad if there were some explicit source saying so - I'd find it interesting! Please share if you know of one.

(note, I used ChatGPT to copy-edit this question because I found it hard to express clearly)

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 0)

From ספר המאמרים תרפ"ה, pg 127 (הבאים ישרש יעקב יציץ ופרח ישראל כו׳):

וזהו ההפרש בחושי הנשמה עצמה בין קודם התלבשותה בגוף לאחר ירידתה והתלבשותה בגוף, דכאשר עודנה למעלה האלקות היא בפשיטות והעולמות הם בהתחדשות, ובירידתה למטה ונתפסת בגוף הנה העולמות הם בפשיטות ואלקות הוא בהתחדשות, ומובן שאינו בערך כלל לכמו שהיתה השגתה תחלה

And this is the difference in the faculties of sensation of the soul itself between before its enclothing in the body and after its descent and enclothing in the body: for when it is still above, Elokus is in peshitus [utter simplicity and obviousness] and the worlds are in his­chadshus [novelty], and in its descent below and its being seized by the body, behold, the worlds are in peshitus and Divinity is in his­chadshus. And it is understood that this is in no comparison at all to how its comprehension originally was.

To the soul's intellectual perception, Hashem's reality is obvious.

questions.title: 14th-18th Centuries Commentaries on Eicha Rabbah
questions.content:
# 14th-18th Centuries Commentaries on Eicha Rabbah ## Frage

I'm looking for commentaries on Eicha Rabbah from the 14th-18th centuries (in print or manuscripts, preferably accessible online). I'm already familiar with Rabbi Shmuel Ashkenazi's Yefeh Anaf, Chida's Kikar La'aden, Rabbi Yissachar Katz's Matnot Kehunah, and Rabbi Naftali Hirtz's commentary (titled simply "פירוש למדרש חמש מגילות"). Are there any others?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 1)

This edition of Eicha Rabbah contains several mefarshim (including all those you mention).

One of those commentaries that fits your timespan is Rabbi Eliyahu Hakohen Itamari the author of Shevet Mussar. He has a commentary entitled V'lo Od Elah. In the standalone sefer (which I have linked) the entry on Eicha Rabbah is not particularly extensive see here, and it would seem that it only focuses on the midrashic instances of the expression "V'lo Od Elah" (hence the title name).

The same sefer above also features the Mishnas Rebbi Eliezer authored by Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda of Pintshov (Pinsk) who lived in the late 17th - early 18th century. (See number 9 on the list of commentaries inside the sefer - on p.2)

### Antwort 2 (Score: 0)

Adding another commentary: Rabbi Shabtai of Rashkov wrote a relatively concise commentary on Eicha Rabbah (as well as the rest of Midrash Rabbah) called אסיפת אמרים. Rabbi Shabtai lived during the 17th-18th centuries (exact dates unclear; he died in 1765). The commentary was first printed in an edition of Eicha Rabbah published in Mahilyow, ca. 1808-1809 (link), and published again in an edition printed in Lviv, 1849 (link). It is largely (and explicitly so) based on past commentaries.

questions.title: Why did Hashem try killing Moses on his way to Egypt?
questions.content:
# Why did Hashem try killing Moses on his way to Egypt? ## Frage

In Exodus Chapter 4:24, Hashem apparently tries to kill Moses. Why? I am ignorant of how the Israelites would have understood this event, and I want to understand it from the Jewish perspective.

(I apologize if my wording is offensive; it is not my intention to offend anyone with my question.)

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 2)

It's complicated. The Mekhilta tells us that Moses promised his father-in-law Jethro that his first son would become an idolater. [Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 18:3] Why? The Midrash says that Jethro first worshipped all existing idols and concluded only God was real [Midrash Tanḥuma, Yitro 7] Rabbi Shim'on Schwab concludes that Jethro wanted a grandson to do as he did: Worship all existing idols and conclude only God was real. This would give him a better appreciation of monotheism. [Mayan Bet Hashoeva on Yitro 18, 4] So Moses at first did not circumcize Gershom, and God threatened to kill him as a result, and his wife Zipporah had to do it in his stead. [Ex. 4:24-26] Moses intentionally did not want Gershom circumcised because of his promise to Jethro.

### Antwort 2 (Score: 2)

Of interest is Rashbam's relevant comments. On the verse in question:

ויפגשהו ה' - המלאך - כי היה מתעצל בהליכתו ומוליך אשתו ובניו.

The LORD encountered him -- [i.e., His] angel -- since Moses was meandered in going, and that he had brought his wife and children along.

The suggestion local to the verse is that Moses' lack of urgency was the cause. However, Rashbam presents a more complex picture elsewhere. Returning to the scene at the bush (Ex. 4:14), he comments

ויחר אף ה' במשה - וחרון אף עשה רושם לפי הפשט כאמור לפנינו: ויפגשהו ה' ויבקש המיתו - כדפירשתי אצל יעקב כשנעשה צולע על יריכו.

The LORD's anger kindled against Moses -- According to the peshat, [God's] anger produces a manifestation as stated later: "Hashem encountered him and sought his death" as I have explained regarding Jacob when his thigh was injured.

Rashbam is implicitly responding to a statement in b. Zevachim 102a (cited by Rashi on our verse) of Rabbi Yehoshua:

רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמֵר: כׇּל חֲרוֹן אַף שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ רוֹשֶׁם, וְזֶה לֹא נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ רוֹשֶׁם

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said: For each instance of [God's] anger in the Torah there is recorded a manifestation, but this instance has no such manifestation.

This is challenged by Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai (in the Bavli, although Rashi quotes Rabbi Yose), who objects:

אַף זֶה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ רוֹשֶׁם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הֲלֹא אַהֲרֹן אָחִיךָ הַלֵּוִי״ – וַהֲלֹא כֹּהֵן הוּא! הָכִי קָאָמַר: אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי אַתָּה כֹּהֵן וְהוּא לֵוִי, עַכְשָׁיו הוּא כֹּהֵן וְאַתָּה לֵוִי.

This, too, has a manifestation, for it says: "Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite?" but in fact he is a priest! [the Bavli clarifies:] That is to say: I intended you will be the priest and he will be the Levite, now he will be the priest and you will be the Levite.

We see that Rashbam rejects the opinion of both the tanna and Rashi and suggests simply that the "manifestation" of God's anger is delayed until later, at the inn. This is distinct from, but thematically agrees with, Rashbam's local comment in the original verse. The consistent position is that Moses' reticence to return to Egypt and accept his mission provokes God's anger. This position is clarified and distilled when we refer back to the episode of Jacob's injury. There (Gen. 32:29), we find:

וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לֹ֤א יַעֲקֹב֙ יֵאָמֵ֥ר עוֹד֙ שִׁמְךָ֔ כִּ֖י אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּֽי־שָׂרִ֧יתָ עִם־אֱלֹהִ֛ים וְעִם־אֲנָשִׁ֖ים וַתּוּכָֽל׃

He [the man] said to him: Your name shall no longer be called Jacob but Israel, for you have striven with God and men and have prevailed.

Rashbam's relevant excerpt:

ומה שלקה יעקב ונצלע, לפי שהקב"ה הבטיחו והוא היה בורח. וכן מצינו בכל ההולכים בדרך שלא ברצון הקב"ה, או ממאנים ללכת שנענשו. במשה כתיב: שלח נא ביד תשלח ויחר אף ה' במשה. ולפי הדרש, אף על פי שאמרו חכמים בכל מקום חרון אף עושה רושם וכאן מה רושם יש? הלא אהרן אחיך הלוי עתיד הוא להיות לוי ואתה כהן ועכשיו הוא יהיה כהן ואתה לוי. אך לפי הפשט: לפי שהיה מתעצל ללכת כתיב: ויהי בדרך במלון ויפגשהו ה' ויבקש המיתו.

The reason that he injured Jacob is that the Holy One promised him [safety], but he had fled [from confronting Esau]. Similarly we find all who travel against the will of the Holy One, or refuse to travel, are punished. Regarding Moses, it is written: "[Moses said,] 'Please, send the one You will send,' and the LORD's anger kindled against Moses." In derash, the Sages said that every instance of [God's] anger has a manifestation, but what manifestation is here? 'Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite' who would only be a Levite while you become the priest? Now, he will be priest and you will be but the Levite." Nevertheless, in peshat, since Moses was reluctant to go, it is written, "It was on the way in the inn, the LORD encountered him and sought his death".

I want to note that this investigation is prototypical Rashbam. He proposes his own principle, "God punishes those who journey/do not journey against His will", and demonstrates its consistency with many textual examples. In service of this principle, he resolves to his satisfaction a claim of the Sages (all instances of God's anger entail a physical manifestation) that ostensibly fails in one textual instance. But in doing so, he rejects the midrashic interpretation of his grandfather and tannaim themselves! This is quite radical, especially for a rishon.

Nevertheless, I do find this explanation of the inn episode compelling. It neatly resolves the mystery by connecting it to the broader narrative while exposing an important characterization of Moses (and God) in these scenes.

### Antwort 3 (Score: -2)

Completely rational question. Moses had two sons Gershom and Eliezer. Circumcision was done on the 8th day and since Gershom was already born in exodus 2 but no mention of Eliezer. This baby must be Eliezer. God commanded Moses to circumcise his son on the 8th day and Tzipporah refused.

Exodus 4.25 Then Zipporah took a flint, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet; and she said: 'Surely a bridegroom of blood art thou to me.'26 So He let him alone. Then she said: 'A bridegroom of blood in regard of the circumcision.'

Here we see clearly she was against it. This is the reason they got divorced. So why did God almost kill Moses? I would argue God almost killed the baby to scare Tzipporah because she was against it, where as Moses was all for it. This explains why they got divorced also. And we know the Midianites believed in other gods according to numbers 25.

Exodus 18.11 Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods; yea, for that they dealt proudly against them.'

Now i know meaning i didn't know before since he worshiped many gods before. Now tzipporah clearly didn't accept the God of Moses as we can tell by her language " a bride groom of blood" .

There is another secret here reguarding the identity of Eliezer and how he became Joshua son of Nun, Moses being Nun. Lets leave that for another discussion.

questions.title: Were Samson's Women his Metaphorical Jawbones?
questions.content:
# Were Samson's Women his Metaphorical Jawbones? ## Frage

The Talmud in Sota 9b states:

״וַיִּבְקַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת הַמַּכְתֵּשׁ אֲשֶׁר בַּלֶּחִי״. אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק דְּבֵי רַבִּי אַמֵּי: הוּא אִיוָּה לְדָבָר טָמֵא — לְפִיכָךְ נִתְלוּ חַיָּיו בְּדָבָר טָמֵא. After Samson smote one thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, he called the place Lehi, and God miraculously granted him to drink, as he was dying of thirst. The verse states: “But God cleaved the hollow place that is in Lehi, and out of there came water; and when he had drunk, his spirit came back, and he revived” (Judges 15:19). Rabbi Yitzḥak of the school of Rabbi Ami says: He desired something unclean, as he was driven by lust to Philistine women. Therefore, the saving of his life was dependent on something unclean, the jawbone of a donkey.

Is the above Talmudic piece suggesting that Samson's women were his metaphorical jawbones? In other words, in the same way that he could have fought the Plishtim bare handed with full trust in God, but, instead, chose to sully himself and rely on a dubious externality (a donkey jawbone), he also could have generally fought the Plishtim in another manner (rather than via connecting with various Plishti women)?

I think the Yerushalmi actually suggests this (Sota First Chapter)

וְאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לֹא יָדְעוּ כִּי מֵיי הִיא כִּי תוֹאָנָה הוּא מְבַקֵּשׁ מִפְּלִשְׁתִּים. אָמַר רִבִּי לָעְזָר. בְּשִׁבְעָה מְקוֹמוֹת כְּתִיב לֹא תִּתְחַתֵּן בָּם. אָמַר רִבִּי אָבִין. לֶאֱסוֹר שִׁבְעָה עַמָּמִין. וְהָכָא הוּא אָמַר הָכֵין. אָמַר רִבִּי יִצְחָק אִם לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ. “And his father and mother did not know that this was from the Eternal, that he was looking for a pretext from the Philistines.” Rebbi Eleazar said, In seven places it is written: “Do not contract marriage with them.” Rebbi Abun said, to prohibit seven peoples. And here, it says so? Rebbi Isaac said, “if he scoffs about the scoffers.”

The Pnei Moshe Explains:

ואת אמר הכין. כי מה' הוא בתמיה: And you say such? That (marrying the Plishti woman) it was from God! (read in astonishment). (Rather the answer is:) אם ללצים הוא יליץ. כתיב דבדרך שאדם רוצה לילך מוליכין אותו: 'With scoffers, He scoffs' it is written. for in the way that a man wants to go, he is led (by God).

Notice it is Rabbi Yitzchak who makes the comment in both Talmuds

questions.title: Devarim vs mitzvot
questions.content:
# Devarim vs mitzvot ## Frage

I am a newcomer to Judaism. When I was younger, it was always emphasised to me that I needed to follow the 10 commandments. But, I've learned that "commandments" in Deut 4/13 may be too strong of a word and, that it's better rendered as sayings/words.

For someone coming from Christendom, what is the difference between the devarim and mitzvot? If I observe the 10 (strictly speaking 7) devarim, does that automatically mean I am also observing the 613 mitzvot?

## Antworten ### ✅ Antwort 1 (Score: 2)

Welcome to Judaism! Let's clear this up step by step:

Are the 10 Commandments actually the 10 Sayings? What's the difference?

Yes, but they are also commandments. In Hebrew, the word for "commandment" is Mitzva. The reason you heard that they are actually the 10 Sayings is because the name given to the 10 Mitzvas given at Mount Sinai are referred to, in Hebrew, as the 10 Devarim (sometimes referred to as Eser HaDiberot). Devarim = "Sayings/Statements" (and this is generally because we heard them spoken by Hashem and Moses during the Sinai Event). That does not mean that they are not also commandments - they are. They are 10 out of the full 613.

That being said there is interesting discussion regarding the word Mitzva (and even Devarim) in our sources and whether "commandment" is the correct translation. If I were to summarise those discussions in a nutshell, Mitzvas are indeed obligations, but they are also ways of connecting to Hashem (the root of the word Mitzva is both Tzav = command as well as Tzavta = connection). Therefore we should view them as more "obligations in a relationship", similar to all relationships. Every relationship carries with it obligations on both sides, but those obligations should be kept lovingly, and with the intention that they are there to bring the participants in the relationship closer.

If I observe the 10 (strictly speaking 7) does that automatically mean I am also observing the 613 Mitzvot?

I can answer for the 10 but I am not sure about the 7. When it comes to the 10, we say that the 10 Devarim contain all of the other Mitzvot within them (see here: 613 mitzvos in the aseres hadibbros), homiletically. In fact we even say that the 10 Devarim are contained in the first, and in fact, in the first word of the first, and in fact, the first letter of the first. This is, as I said, homiletics. One should not stick to the 10 Devarim and ignore the rest, practically. This homiletical teaching is beautiful and contains many secrets, but practically speaking it just means that if one truly internalises the 10 Devarim, that will lead to them keeping the rest as well, and in some deep way they are all connected to the 10.

That being said, this applies to a Jew. To a Noahide, I am not sure what there is to be said about keeping the 7. We generally hold that the non-Jew is not obligated to keep the 613 (and actually forbidden from keeping some, such as Shabbat - which is included in the 10), and I am unaware of any homiletical interpretations that keeping the 7 is equivalent to keeping the 613, but could be. The 7 bring the non-Jew closer to God and fulfil his obligations to Him, and they do so on their own.

I have provided quite a few links to a reputable, authentic resource for questions on Judaism, to back up and expand on what I've been saying - Chabad.org, who are on top of their game generally speaking. Here are a few others about the Noahide Laws for you to read up on.

https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/62221/jewish/The-7-Noahide-Laws.htm

https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/5559665/jewish/The-Seven-Laws-of-Noah.htm

https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/4157474/jewish/Seven-Laws-for-a-Beautiful-Planet.htm

https://www.chabad.org/kabbalah/article_cdo/aid/380332/jewish/The-Mitzvot-of-Non-Jews.htm

questions.title: Does reading the Judges of Caesarea's formulas as area-based fit the Gemara's flow in Sukkah 8b?
questions.content:
# Does reading the Judges of Caesarea's formulas as area-based fit the Gemara's flow in Sukkah 8b? ## Frage

In Sukkah 8b, the Gemara cites the “Judges of Caesarea” who said: A circle inscribed in a square is one-quarter, a square inscribed in a circle is one-half.

Typically, this is read as a statement about perimeters, but Tosafot already notes difficulties with this reading. So, I was exploring whether perhaps they meant for us to calculate the areas, not the perimeters:

The inscribed circle is ~25% smaller in area than its square (actual value ≈ 21.46%). The inscribed square of that circle is exactly 50% smaller in area than its circumscribing square.

A circle inscribed in a square is [approximately] one-quarter [less than the area of the circumscribing square. While the area of] a square inscribed in a circle is [exactly] one-half [less than the circumscribing square of the circle].

If so, the Gemara could be read as first offering an approximate formula of the Judges (like Rabbi Yochanan’s method) that is “good enough” when it leads to a stringency, alongside their precise one for calculating the area of the internal square of a round sukkah to complement Rabbi Yochanan's imprecise method that utilizes circumference; or even the Gemara's own use of a circle's diameter to calculate the perimeter of the internal square of a round sukkah, Sukkah 8b.

It seems the Gemara may have brought the first saying of the Judges of Caesarea in support of Rabbi Yochanan right after the discussion about how his formula was an acceptable method even though it was imprecise, so long as it resulted in a stringency. It supported him by showing that even the Judges of Caesarea stated that a circle inscribed in a square has an area which is one-quarter less than the area of the external square when it is actually 21.46% less.

That said, the Gemara ends the discussion with bringing the second part of the sayings of the Judges of Caesarea to teach us how to more simply calculate the area of a square inside a circle (round sukkah) without having to use the formulas for circumference or the diagonal of a square for calculating its perimeter. And their formula is also exactly precise.

For example, if you wanted to know if a round sukkah is valid all you need to do is draw a square on the outside of the round sukkah and then measure the length of one side and square it. Afterwards, you know that the area of the square inside the circle is exactly half the area of the external square of that same circle. So, if one side of the external square is 6 amos then the total area of the external square would be 36 amos and the round sukkah would contain an internal square of 18 amos, exactly 50% the external square.

I want to read Gemara 8a like this: This is where R Yochanan was imprecise in his measurement, and his imprecision results in a stringency. [The Gemara then notes for the reader how it knows that an imprecision resulting in a stringency is an acceptable practice and that it had indeed arrived at the proper understanding of R Yochanan’s formula by bringing the following proof:] The Rabbis of Caesarea and some say the Judges of Caesarea… A circle inscribed in a square is one-quarter less… But this [formula also] is not so [exact] for we see that it is not that great [resulting in a stringency].

Therefore, the Judges of Caesarea were correct and the Gemara knew why it was bringing their formulas.

My question: Does this reinterpretation fit the logical flow of the Gemara — or am I forcing the text?

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 0)

This is a very niche question as one needs to have learned the sugya in depth to understand it. I happen to have just done so - which attracted me to your question. Your suggestion is mathematically correct, but how does this help R Yochanan? R Yochanan is interested in placing people all across the circumference of the circle - or even if you say he is interested in placing them inside the circle, he would want to fill all of the circle.

In any case, as Tosfot notes, the statement of the Judges of Caesarea don't really help us because they are incorrect, at least as it relates to the circumference of the Sukkah.

What is interesting to note is that the area of the circle going around a 4x4 sukkah is exactly 24 ! If anything, that might have been what R Yochanan meant (problem is the gemara doesn't seem to think this way, but the fact Rashi and Tosfot both allude to areas - while the gemara only speak of circumference - might mean they also explored this)

questions.title: Why is Nedarim in Nashim?
questions.content:
# Why is Nedarim in Nashim? ## Frage

Simple question surprised not asked yet, but why is tractate Nedarim in order Nashim? I am not presuming it has anywhere better to be, but I don't see how it directly connects with Nashim more than other orders.

## Antworten ### ✅ Antwort 1 (Score: 8)

The Gemara in Sota 2A mentions this question and gives an answer that it continues from the seventh perek in Kesubos that discusses Nedarim:

וְלִיתְנֵי סוֹטָה, וַהֲדַר לִיתְנֵי נָזִיר! אַיְּידֵי דִּתְנָא כְּתוּבּוֹת וּתְנָא ״הַמַּדִּיר״, תְּנָא נְדָרִים. וְאַיְּידֵי דִּתְנָא נְדָרִים — תְּנָא נָזִיר, דְּדָמֵי לִנְדָרִים. וְקָתָנֵי סוֹטָה, כִּדְרַבִּי.

The Gemara asks: But if so, let him teach tractate Sota first and then let him teach tractate Nazir, which is the way these topics are ordered in the Torah, and also accords better with the statement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The Gemara answers: Since the tanna taught tractate Ketubot, and in that tractate he taught a chapter that begins: One who vows, in which there are several mishnayot concerning vows between husbands and wives, he then taught tractate Nedarim, whose subject is the halakhot of vows. And since he taught tractate Nedarim, he then taught tractate Nazir, which is similar to tractate Nedarim in that one becomes a nazirite by taking a vow. And he then teaches tractate Sota, in accordance with the statement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi

### Antwort 2 (Score: 3)

As I discuss in this article, Nashim is perhaps not the most accurate title for the Seder. Yes, it captures an aspect of many of the masechtot therein. Yet if that were the sole grouping principle, I would have expected e.g. Niddah in that grouping.

If I had to give the Seder a name / grouping principle, I would have labeled it Kinyanim and Kabbalot, Acquisitions and Acceptances. Kiddushin is not actually about betrothal but, as the perakim continue, about all sorts of kinyanim.

### Antwort 3 (Score: 2)

Nedarim appears in the Torah primarily with regard to women.

The sole pasuk (3) dealing with men's utterances functions more as an introduction to those of women (4-17)

When the parsha wraps up it doesn't even mention those of a man (17)

וַיְדַבֵּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל־רָאשֵׁ֣י הַמַּטּ֔וֹת לִבְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר זֶ֣ה הַדָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֖ר צִוָּ֥ה יְ־הֹוָֽה׃ (ג) אִישׁ֩ כִּֽי־יִדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר לַֽי־הֹוָ֗ה אֽוֹ־הִשָּׁ֤בַע שְׁבֻעָה֙ לֶאְסֹ֤ר אִסָּר֙ עַל־נַפְשׁ֔וֹ לֹ֥א יַחֵ֖ל דְּבָר֑וֹ כְּכׇל־הַיֹּצֵ֥א מִפִּ֖יו יַעֲשֶֽׂה׃ (ד) וְאִשָּׁ֕ה כִּֽי־תִדֹּ֥ר נֶ֖דֶר לַי־הֹוָ֑ה וְאָסְרָ֥ה אִסָּ֛ר בְּבֵ֥ית אָבִ֖יהָ בִּנְעֻרֶֽיהָ׃ (ה) וְשָׁמַ֨ע אָבִ֜יהָ אֶת־נִדְרָ֗הּ וֶֽאֱסָרָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָֽסְרָ֣ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֔הּ וְהֶחֱרִ֥ישׁ לָ֖הּ אָבִ֑יהָ וְקָ֙מוּ֙ כׇּל־נְדָרֶ֔יהָ וְכׇל־אִסָּ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אָסְרָ֥ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ יָקֽוּם׃ (ו) וְאִם־הֵנִ֨יא אָבִ֣יהָ אֹתָהּ֮ בְּי֣וֹם שׇׁמְעוֹ֒ כׇּל־נְדָרֶ֗יהָ וֶֽאֱסָרֶ֛יהָ אֲשֶׁר־אָסְרָ֥ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ לֹ֣א יָק֑וּם וַֽי־הֹוָה֙ יִֽסְלַח־לָ֔הּ כִּי־הֵנִ֥יא אָבִ֖יהָ אֹתָֽהּ׃ (ז) וְאִם־הָי֤וֹ תִֽהְיֶה֙ לְאִ֔ישׁ וּנְדָרֶ֖יהָ עָלֶ֑יהָ א֚וֹ מִבְטָ֣א שְׂפָתֶ֔יהָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָסְרָ֖ה עַל־נַפְשָֽׁהּ׃ (ח) וְשָׁמַ֥ע אִישָׁ֛הּ בְּי֥וֹם שׇׁמְע֖וֹ וְהֶחֱרִ֣ישׁ לָ֑הּ וְקָ֣מוּ נְדָרֶ֗יהָ וֶֽאֱסָרֶ֛הָ אֲשֶׁר־אָסְרָ֥ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ יָקֻֽמוּ׃ (ט) וְ֠אִ֠ם בְּי֨וֹם שְׁמֹ֣עַ אִישָׁהּ֮ יָנִ֣יא אוֹתָהּ֒ וְהֵפֵ֗ר אֶת־נִדְרָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלֶ֔יהָ וְאֵת֙ מִבְטָ֣א שְׂפָתֶ֔יהָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָסְרָ֖ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֑הּ וַי־הֹוָ֖ה יִֽסְלַֽח־לָֽהּ׃ (י) וְנֵ֥דֶר אַלְמָנָ֖ה וּגְרוּשָׁ֑ה כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־אָסְרָ֥ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ יָק֥וּם עָלֶֽיהָ׃ (יא) וְאִם־בֵּ֥ית אִישָׁ֖הּ נָדָ֑רָה אֽוֹ־אָסְרָ֥ה אִסָּ֛ר עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ בִּשְׁבֻעָֽה׃ (יב) וְשָׁמַ֤ע אִישָׁהּ֙ וְהֶחֱרִ֣שׁ לָ֔הּ לֹ֥א הֵנִ֖יא אֹתָ֑הּ וְקָ֙מוּ֙ כׇּל־נְדָרֶ֔יהָ וְכׇל־אִסָּ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אָסְרָ֥ה עַל־נַפְשָׁ֖הּ יָקֽוּם׃ (יג) וְאִם־הָפֵר֩ יָפֵ֨ר אֹתָ֥ם ׀ אִישָׁהּ֮ בְּי֣וֹם שׇׁמְעוֹ֒ כׇּל־מוֹצָ֨א שְׂפָתֶ֧יהָ לִנְדָרֶ֛יהָ וּלְאִסַּ֥ר נַפְשָׁ֖הּ לֹ֣א יָק֑וּם אִישָׁ֣הּ הֲפֵרָ֔ם וַי־הֹוָ֖ה יִֽסְלַֽח־לָֽהּ׃ (יד) כׇּל־נֵ֛דֶר וְכׇל־שְׁבֻעַ֥ת אִסָּ֖ר לְעַנֹּ֣ת נָ֑פֶשׁ אִישָׁ֥הּ יְקִימֶ֖נּוּ וְאִישָׁ֥הּ יְפֵרֶֽנּוּ׃ (טו) וְאִם־הַחֲרֵשׁ֩ יַחֲרִ֨ישׁ לָ֥הּ אִישָׁהּ֮ מִיּ֣וֹם אֶל־יוֹם֒ וְהֵקִים֙ אֶת־כׇּל־נְדָרֶ֔יהָ א֥וֹ אֶת־כׇּל־אֱסָרֶ֖יהָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלֶ֑יהָ הֵקִ֣ים אֹתָ֔ם כִּי־הֶחֱרִ֥שׁ לָ֖הּ בְּי֥וֹם שׇׁמְעֽוֹ׃ (טז) וְאִם־הָפֵ֥ר יָפֵ֛ר אֹתָ֖ם אַחֲרֵ֣י שׇׁמְע֑וֹ וְנָשָׂ֖א אֶת־עֲוֺנָֽהּ׃ (יז) אֵ֣לֶּה הַֽחֻקִּ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֤ה יְ־הֹוָה֙ אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֔ה בֵּ֥ין אִ֖ישׁ לְאִשְׁתּ֑וֹ בֵּֽין־אָ֣ב לְבִתּ֔וֹ בִּנְעֻרֶ֖יהָ בֵּ֥ית אָבִֽיהָ׃

questions.title: Does Isaiah 47:2’s use of showq refer to the thigh or shin?
questions.content:
# Does Isaiah 47:2’s use of showq refer to the thigh or shin? ## Frage

Isaiah 47:1–3 has the “virgin daughter of Babylon” uncovering the showq, and her ‘ervah is uncovered. It seems to me at first glance that the reason her ‘ervah is uncovered is simply because she removed her skirt. But if this passage teaches that the showq is ‘ervah, then we better know what showq means. I’ve seen translations render it “thigh,” but some lexicons say the word actually refers to the “shin” when referencing humans.

What specifically does showq mean in Isaiah 47:2? Do women with knee‐length clothing expose ‘ervah according to this passage?

questions.title: Why does 1 Samuel 16:10-11 say Jesse had 8 sons, while 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 mentions 7?
questions.content:
# Why does 1 Samuel 16:10-11 say Jesse had 8 sons, while 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 mentions 7? ## Frage

Curious what the meaning behind this is and/or if any early Jewish commentators address this.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 0)

As Metzudat David on Samuel 1:16:10 noted, it's possible that there indeed was an eighth brother, Elihu, mentioned only in Chronicles 1:27:18. According to Tanchuma Vayera 25 (mentioned by the Metzudah), Elihu was the only sibling who survived the king of Moab's killing of David's family. Other commentators (e.g. Radak, Ralbag, Rabbi Steinsaltz) however, have argued that Elihu was either a second name of one of David's other brothers (Ralbag and Rabbi Steinsaltz suggested specifically Elihu, likely due to the similarities between the names, and the logic behind promoting David's eldest brother to an important administratorial position), or the name of a nephew (and therefore not a "brother" in the regular sense, but a kinsman).

So why were only seven sons mentioned in the beginning of Chronicles? A few commentators have addressed the issue:

The commentary by the anonymous Student of Rasag on Chronicles 1:2:15 suggested:

"דויד השביעי – ואעפ"י שעוד אליהו שמיני כדכתיב בדברי הימים: ליהודה אליהו מאחי דויד (דברי הימים א כ"ז:י"ח), ותימה לבני אדם למה אמר דויד השביעי, ואומר ודוד הוא הקטן (שמואל א י"ז:י"ד), דע לך כי אליהו היה באותה שעה קטן ומוטל בעריסה בחיק אומנתו ולפיכך לא מנה אותו בחלק הבנים, ומניין אתה יודע שכן הוא הדבר, כי בשעה שברח דוד מפני שאול הנהיג עמו אחיו ובית אביו כדכתיב וינחם את פני מלך מואב (שמואל א כ"ב:ד') וכשהלך מאתו קם מלך מואב והרגן כולם ולא נשתייר מהם אלא אליהו שהיה קטן ותטמנהו אומנתו, ולפי שקטן היה לא העלהו כאן בחשבון הבנים, וכן דרשו חכמים (ילקוט שמעוני שמואל קמ"ז). ויהודה בן קורייש פירש כי לאליאב היה בן גדול והעבירו ישי לפני שמואל, ועוד נשאר הקטן הוא דוד, ולכך אומר ויעבר ישי שבעת בניו (שמואל א ט"ז:י') ודוד הוא שמיני, כי בן אליאב חשוב בבנים..."

"David the seventh - and even though Elihu was the remaining eighth, as it is written in Chronicles: "Of Judah, Elihu from the brothers of David" (Chronicles 1:27:18), and it is therefore strange why it is written that David is the seventh (and no more), and it is also stated that "and David was the youngest" (Samuel 1:17:14), know that Elihu at the time was young and lay in the crib by his nurse and therefore was not counted among the sons, and how do you know that this was the case? Because when David fled from Shaul he led his brothers and the house of his father, as it is written "So he led them to the king of Moab" (Samuel 1:22:4), and when he left, the king of Moab rose and killed all of them, and none remained but Elihu who was small and hidden by his nurse, and since he was small, he was not counted among the sons, and the sages also taught (Yalkut Shimoni Samuel 147). And Yehudah Kuraish explained that Eliav had a grownup son who was passed by Yishai before Shmuel, and "another remains, the youngest, David", and for this reason it is stated that Yishai passed his seven sons (Samuel 1:16:10), and David was the eigthth, because Eliav's son was counted among the sons..."

Pseudo-Rashi on the verse in Chronicles 1:2:15 suggested:

"דויד השבעי – מלא יו"ד מפני כבודו של דוד ועתה מצא המרגלית לפיכך לא מנה השמיני אליהו."

"David the seventh - written fully with a Yod1 in honor of David, as he (i.e., the author of the text) now came across the gemstone and therefore did not name the eighth, Elihu."

Malbim on Chronicles 1:2:15:

"דויד השביעי – וזה סותר למה שבשמואל (א' טז, י; י"ז:י"ב) חושב לישי שמונה בנים ודוד הוא הקטן. ודעת חז"ל במדרש שהשמיני הוא אליהו הנזכר בין הנגידים שהקים דוד על יהודה, אליהו אחי דוד (לקמן כ"ז:י"ח), והוא היה קטן מדוד, וקרא לדוד קטן על שהיה מקטין א״ע, וכן פרש"י. וראב"ע ורד"ק פירשו שאליהו היה אח מן האב ולא מן האם, ולכן לא חשבו פה מפני שאומר ואחיותיהם צרויה ואביגיל, והם היו אחיות מן האם ולא מן האב, וא"כ לא היו אחיות לאליהו לא מן האב ולא מן האם, וכדבריהם נראה ממ״ש (שמואל ב י"ז:כ"ה) ועמשא בן איש ושמו יתרא הישראלי אשר בא אל אביגיל בת נחש אחות צרויה אם יואב, מבואר (לפי הפשט, והדרש ידוע) שאביגיל היתה בת נחש לא בת ישי, וא״כ היתה אחותם רק מן האם, לכן אמר אחות צרויה ולא אמר אחות דוד, מפני שאחות צרויה היתה מן האב ומן האם שגם צרויה היתה בת נחש, ואמם נשאת לישי באלמנותה."

"David the seventh - and this contradicts what is said in Samuel (1:16:10, 17:12) that Yishai was thought to have eight sons and David was the youngest. And our sages' opinion in the midrash is that the eighth was Elihu, mentioned among the princes that David raised "Of Judah, Elihu from the brothers of David" (ibid. 27:18), and he was younger than David, but the text called David the youngest because he made himself small (i.e., he was humble), and so explained Rashi. And Ibn Ezra and Radak explained that Elihu was a brother from the paternal side but not from the maternal side, and therefore he was not counted here, as it is said "and their sisters Tzeruyah and Avigail", and they were sisters on the maternal side and not the paternal side, and therefore were not sisters of Elihu not from the father and not from the mother, and their arguments appear to be proven from what is written (Samuel 2:17:25), "And Amassah was the son of a man named Yitra the Israelite who cohabited with Avigail daughter of Nachash" - not the daughter of Yishai, and therefore was only their sister from the maternal side, and therefore it is written "sister of Tzruyah", not "sister of David", since she was the sister of Tzruyah from father and mother, since Tzruyah was also the daughter of Nachash, and their mother married Yishai during her widowhood."

1 Unclear to me whether he meant that David was written with a Yod (דויד) or that he had before him seventh written with two Yods (שביעי) rather than what we have (שבעי).

questions.title: Quote about not answering Amen before Modim

questions.title: Punishments that "never happened and could never happen" - weakens the perceived authority/seriousness of the Torah?
questions.content:
# Punishments that "never happened and could never happen" - weakens the perceived authority/seriousness of the Torah? ## Frage

I think the title is bad but I am having a "bad articulation day" - feel free to edit.

What I am trying to ask is this: if we have some punishment-involving-Mitzvot that are recognised as being "impossible" and "will never happen", such as the ones recorded here, based on Sanhedrin 71a: Why would the Torah give us mitzvot that will never actually happen?

  • Ben Sorer u'Morer (wayward son)
  • Ir HaNidachat (idolatrous city)
  • Bet HaMenuga (leprous house)
  • Sotah (suspected wife) (this probably did happen, but there is an opinion that it didn't)

... then the question is, how does this not weaken the authority of the Torah, at least in the minds of some? If a parent threatens a consequence to an action, and the child performs the action repeatedly but never receives the consequence (the parent always find a loophole, as did the courts for these Mitzvot), the child eventually starts to lose respect for the parent's authority, right? Or wrong? Maybe the opposite is true.

I am not looking for site users' own opinions on this, but actual sources that ask the question that I ask, and answer it. I admit, it's not the world's greatest question, and there are some obvious answers but I want to see them from the pen of a generational scholar.

For the record, I don't personally think the Torah's authority should be or is weakened by this, but I still would like to know if it's dealt with because it is a valid question, and a serious one to some degree - it's well known that by their inclusion in the Torah, non-Jewish/non-"Rabbinic" bible followers, such as Christians, did "keep" them with horrific consequences.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 1)

Even though the OP sounds interesting, its basic setup is completely flawed to begin with. Therefore, there is no special response needed. We must merely identify the false pretense.

A. These mitzvos certainly do happen.

B. There is no lack or weakening of authority at all.

  1. The "wayward son", way before he faces a question of execution, is given 39 lashes with a fierce whip by the Court, for his "first offense" of stealing his father's funds and eating and drinking with the stolen funds. This itself (the lashes), could kill and is not covered by the Talmudic guarantee that there will never be such a case.

The case that will never be is direct execution when the son commits a highly defined act of theft of his father's funds and eating meat and wine in a glutenous fashion purchased from those funds under peculiar circumstances, a "second time" within 3 months.

wayward sons also suffer public humiliation etc.

The OP forgets that these sins do get punished, just not punished in the most extreme way possible due to technicalities of the law.

  1. Idolaters that convert or pervert their neighbors are likewise killed by Torah Law all the time. The question is if an entire town in certain extreme ways could all become classified as such extreme idolaters as to have the town burned down by the Court etc.

  2. People who practice evil speech and gossip (among some other sins) are punished in Torah Law. They usually contract white skin blotches which cause them to dwell outside the camp and call out "unclean" to passersby until a Cohen says they are cured.

This really did happen.

What might not happen is that the entire family has to demolish their impure house due to such levels of gossip that the "walls have ears" and the walls couldn't take it anymore. However the Cohen does come to inspect the house and colored blotches did appear on houses.

  1. People who act lewdly within marriage and risk the sanctity of their marriage certainly existed and were punished via forced divorce, ruined reputations and humiliations etc., and yes, execution if applicable.

The Sotah procedures did occur in the Temple. Women did go through it and some ended up being punished. The question is did a woman actually need to publicly rot and explode miraculously as a curse among her people under very technical rules and events?

All these people face punishment and loss for their bad deeds.

No one is escaping justice.

All of these mitzvos still apply to us.

The Rambam codifies the wayward son as a mitzvah that we not eat like gluttons which could lead towards becoming like a classic wayward son.

Likewise the Torah commands us not to commit idolatry and not to preach idolatrty as well as to avoid evil gossip and to avoid adulterous activity and flirtations.

And yes, there are smaller and greater punishments along these paths so that no one would assume the authority of the Torah is weakening.

The OP makes it sound like these special mitzvos are completely irrational, non-existent theory, and never punishable, and not practiced or taught. It obviously is not the case.

Saying that the Torah's authority is "weakening" because of technicalities in extreme cases, would be like claiming that murderers are flocking from Florida to Texas because they realized they could merely receive lethal injection if caught in Texas, vs. the electric chair back in Florida.

Maybe the OP should restart and ask why these extreme cases are taught when we already have a Torah framework for their sins, and what lessons they teach if they will never come to pass?

### Antwort 2 (Score: 0)

The answer to your question is simply "Yes". These cases will cause some people to question the authority of the Torah and weaken its validity in their eyes. But that's not a "Torah" problem. That's a "That Guy" problem.

The Passuk in Hosea 14:10 says:

מִ֤י חָכָם֙ וְיָ֣בֵֽן אֵ֔לֶּה נָב֖וֹן וְיֵדָעֵ֑ם כִּֽי־יְשָׁרִ֞ים דַּרְכֵ֣י יְהֹוָ֗ה וְצַדִּקִים֙ יֵ֣לְכוּ בָ֔ם וּפֹשְׁעִ֖ים יִכָּ֥שְׁלוּ בָֽם׃

The wise will consider these words,

The prudent will take note of them.

For the paths of GOD are smooth;

The righteous can walk on them,

While sinners stumble on them.

People ultimately have free will and can interpret anything they want however they want. That doesn't mean they are interpreting it correctly, and it also doesn't mean that the One making the statement is giving it over incorrectly.

Hashem wrote the Torah in a specific way, meant to be interpreted through the Oral Torah and the commentaries. There will always be people who misread things (whether willfully or mistakenly), and the onus is on them to correct themselves, not to bend the Torah to fit their philosophy.

The Torah is right, it's up to us to realize it.

questions.title: Shlosh Meyos Chamishim V'Chameish (355) - mi yodeya?
questions.content:
# Shlosh Meyos Chamishim V'Chameish (355) - mi yodeya? ## Frage

Who knows three hundred fifty-five? Besides the obvious, שנה, year/change/repeat/review/digest, unless you can expand on that one.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 4)

1 - I noticed an observation in נחלת אבות - ספר שופטים (אברהם בלוי, תשמ"ה) on p. 26 (p. 42 in Otzar and past the free 40 page limit) that the period of the שופטים lasted 355 years. This begins with the passing of יהושע in the year 2,516 and ends with the passing of עלי הכהן in the year 2,871.

This way to define the שופטים period seems to be in line with the words of the Meiri at the beginning of Pirkei Avos:

ואמר שיהושע בעת מותו מסרה לאותם הזקנים ועתניאל בן קנז היה מראשוניהם ועלי הכהן מאחרוניהם עד זמן החרבן שהשופטים אף הם בכלל הזקנים כמו שביארנו בפתיחה ומהם נמסרה לנביאים שהרי שמואל מראשוניהם

See below for the full excerpt from the sefer:

2 - If you want a bit of a stretch, we see a multiple of 355 in the Torah with the count in במדבר having 3,550 men over and above the number 600,000. Those 3,550 had a meaningful impact in the silver donated to the משכן for the collection of the half-shekel. The 300,000 shekalim corresponding to the 600,000 men were used for the silver אדנים of the משכן and the remaining 1,775 (corresponding to the 3,550 men) were used specifically for the silver hooks, coatings and wrappings of the posts of the courtyard.

(שמות לח:כח) וְאֶת הָאֶ֜לֶף וּשְׁבַ֤ע הַמֵּאוֹת֙ וַחֲמִשָּׁ֣ה וְשִׁבְעִ֔ים עָשָׂ֥ה וָוִ֖ים לָעַמּוּדִ֑ים וְצִפָּ֥ה רָאשֵׁיהֶ֖ם וְחִשַּׁ֥ק אֹתָֽם

One can also consider that 3,550 as 355 עדות of men (where a minyan is 10).

3 - As implied in the original question, if you search around there are many who comment on the gematria of שנה = 355 in various ways as that's by far the most frequent occurrence of a word with a value of 355 in Tanach. Indeed the longest non-leap year in the current Jewish calendar is 355 days. There are also many who comment on פרעה which is by far the 2nd most frequent occurrence of 355 in Tanach. I will leave it up to others who desire to expand upon these.

### Antwort 2 (Score: 1)

355 is Gematria

פצפצי"ה

Which is one of the names seventy names of the MT"T according to Alef Bet of R Akiva.

This name occurs in the Petek, at the end of the ninth line.

It is also

נ נח נחמ נחמן

with the addition of 1 kollel. This name is on the seventh line of the Petek.

questions.title: Transliterated Sephardic siddur
questions.content:
# Transliterated Sephardic siddur ## Frage

I'm looking for an Edot HaMizrach Siddur with a Latin-script transliteration.

The Siddur should be user-friendly, and have weekday and Shabbos davening. The transliteration should preferably fit with the pronunciation of Bukharian Jews.

I know Artscroll has a very good one, but that is Nusach Ashkenaz.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 4)

You might want to try the Siddur Ner Tamid:

Introducing the exquisite Siddur Ner Tamid: Sephardic Jewish Siddur, a meticulously crafted prayerbook designed to unite and inspire worshippers across the globe. This exceptional volume is thoughtfully divided into two parts, catering to both Shabbat and Weekday prayers, making it a versatile companion for spiritual seekers. Masterfully transliterated, it provides an inclusive experience for individuals from all backgrounds, empowering them to join in with other communities and strengthen the bonds of faith. This remarkable Siddur has garnered international acclaim, with copies cherished by devotees in the U.S., Israel, Spain, the U.K., Germany, France, Poland, and India. Embrace this treasured prayerbook and revel in the unity it brings to the diverse tapestry of Sephardic Jewish communities worldwide.

Here is a sample page posted on the Amazon page:

### Antwort 2 (Score: 1)

In addition to Siddur Ner Tamid, which is indeed what I would recommend seeing as you prefer Latin-script transliteration, there is also Siddur Lev Eliezer, available from Eichler's, Seforim Center, and others. Lev Eliezer seems to follow the customs of Syrian Jews, and while I purchased it, I found the formatting and transliteration choices personally difficult to use (אֵי- transliterated as -íye, for example).

I am unaware of any other English-transliterated siddurim. I am aware of a French-transliterated siddur from the Patah Eliyahou series. However, Patah Eliyahou I believe follows more closely to North African customs and the Livorno nusach.

(I assume OP is aware of Siddur Tefilat Azaria, which is a Bukharian siddur, but transliterated using Cyrillic script, given that OP specified Latin-script transliteration.)

questions.title: Why are red tzitzit assur to Ashkenazi?
questions.content:
# Why are red tzitzit assur to Ashkenazi? ## Frage

First question so pardon me. Will try to follow the rules.

Recently moved and got to a mostly ashkenazi shul and am sephardic. I understand Ashkenazim only wear white tzitzit as their minhag but I heard that specifically red is also additionally assur.

I am curious of the logic and am not able to find any reason for the custom. I even asked my rabbi and he was unaware beyond ashkenazi wear only white.

I myself have tzitzit in a few other colors to match a tallit gadol and katan and see where Rambam states if a garment is red it ought have red tzitzit.

If helpful, I do have my rabbis permission to wear my non white tzitzit which are black and green.

Thanks for any insight.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 1)

According to Ashkenazi custom, as cited by the Rema (YD 178:1), wearing red clothes is forbidden as an aspect of avoiding the emulation of immodest gentile practices.

The congregants/rabbi you spoke with were likely referring to this, as red strands would presumably only be worn by you with a dominantly red garment (per the Rambam in H. Sisith 2:8).

questions.title: Is there a comprehensive sefer on the Jecke pronunciation of Hebrew?
questions.content:
# Is there a comprehensive sefer on the Jecke pronunciation of Hebrew? ## Frage

Is there a comprehensive sefer on the Jecke pronunciation of Hebrew?

I’d prefer one in English, but Hebrew one/s is fine.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 4)

While several poskim address pronunciation, there is no comprehensive work on the subject of German havoroh (pronunciation).

  • R' Binyomin Shlomo Hamburger devotes a chapter in his Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz to the pronunciation of the chaulom/cholom vowel (Vol. 1, Ch. 9) although my friend, Dr. Gabriel Wasserman, questions the validity of some of his assertions, since the phonology of Western Yiddish had a long /O/, whereas German does not, the development of the distinctive chaulom had more to do with language shifts over the 19th century than regional pronunciation, as R' Hamburger asserts.

  • The Yosef Ometz (R' Josef Hahn, a dayan under the Sheloh) and the Pnei Yehoshua' (R' Jakob Jehoschua-Falk, R' Dovid Schiff Londoner's rov) both complain about the loss of certain phonemic distinctions in their respective time periods, namely the loss of ח–כֿ and א–ע distinctions, which indicates that, at least in Frankfurt, these values were preserved at a fairly late date, relative to other Ashkenazi communities.

The best source for [late] Jekkisch havoroh is in the numerous recordings of Shoah survivors, including Messrs. Benno Weis and Moshe Schnerb, along with Chazzan Robert Frankel זכרונם לברכה. Herr Weis, in particular, left a large legacy, including complete Tauroh, haftoroh, Esther, and Eichoh leinen for the entire year, the seder, and nuschaos for most special tefillos, as they were sung in Frankfurt.

Sources:

Hamburger, R' Binyomin Shlomo. Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz Cheilek I (Bnei Brak).

Wasserman, Dr. Gabriel. Personal communications with the author.

Strauß, R' Sidney. Personal communications with the author. 2019

Recordings:

Chazzan Frankel: Khal Adath Jeshurun, Washington Heights

Herr Schnerb: Khal Adath Jeshurun, Washington Heights

Herr Weis: KAJ, Zemiros Ashkenaz, Dartmouth Jewish Sound Archive

questions.title: Requirements for Washing Hands
questions.content:
# Requirements for Washing Hands ## Frage

When do you need to wash hands 3 times and with a vessel? It is my understanding that waking up in the morning requires 3 times and from a vessel. But what about:

  1. After using a restroom
  2. Touching your nose or face
  3. Grabbing something from the floor
  4. Touching the floor

I ask about these because I do these during the work day and I can't wash my hands with a vessel at work.

## Antworten ### Antwort 1 (Score: 0)

In the Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim (4:18), there is a list of things from which you need to wash your hands. The Magen Avraham quotes earlier sources who says that those things (including after using the restroom, but not the rest) do not require three times.

However, there are others, mentioned in the Shaarei Teshuva, that do hold of washing three times. The Ben Ish Chai as well holds this way, and even that you need to switch back and forth just as in the morning.

And so, being that the Mishnah Berurah frames the Magen Avraham as the final word on this, you wouldn't need to wash three times for the restroom. But this would ultimately come down to community's customs.

All this is about the amount of times and whether or not you need to wash in a right-left pattern. As for using a vessel, it would likely depend on the reason. Those things that are because of cleanliness, you can wash any way you'd like. This goes for the second item on your list. As for the restroom, since there is an element of Ruach Ra, or evil spirit, it does seem that a vessel is required for that, but you don't need to worry about where you wash into: it can be spilled anywhere.

However, on this too, there are those who say that any washing is fine, these days, since our restrooms are not similar to those of which the sages have spoken of.
